screens.title: Calculus and Differential Equations for Robotics
screens.narratorSegment: In robotics, calculus is the language that turns sensor readings into motion and control. In this chapter you will connect position, velocity, and acceleration as vector derivatives, learn how angular velocity drives orientation through a skew-symmetric matrix, and see how ordinary differential equations describe dynamics. You will also compare simple numerical integrators like Euler to higher-order methods like RK4, and run practical MATLAB simulations with ode45. These tools let you predict and test behavior before you run hardware, and they explain why some simulations explode while others remain stable. For example, a small time step in Euler's method may track a damped oscillator well, but a larger step can diverge and produce physically impossible energy growth. We will also examine rotating frames and the Coriolis term, which matter for quadrotors and any rotating mechanism. By the end, you will be able to set up the ODE for a mass-spring-damper, run an integration step, and reason about stability and solver choice. Consider the central idea: motion is derivatives, and derivatives integrated correctly give you reliable simulations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives map directly to practical robotics tasks. First, you will compute derivatives and integrals of vector-valued functions to convert position signals into velocity and acceleration used by controllers and filters. Second, you will set up ordinary differential equations that model robot dynamics, expressing states and control inputs so you can reason about time evolution. Third, you will use numerical integrators such as Euler and Runge-Kutta to simulate dynamics in MATLAB and observe how step size affects accuracy. Fourth, you will understand velocity in rotating frames and the Coriolis contribution so you can correctly transform sensor data between body and inertial coordinates. Each objective explains a skill and why it matters: derivatives connect sensors to control; ODEs let you encode mechanics; numerical methods let you test algorithms offline; rotating-frame kinematics prevent errors in orientation-dependent forces. As you progress, you will see short examples and implement a damped oscillator simulation to verify understanding and experience stability trade-offs firsthand.

screens.title: Position, Velocity, Acceleration as Vector Derivatives
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: position is a vector-valued function p(t) = [x(t), y(t), z(t)]^T that gives location in space over time. Velocity is its first derivative, v(t) = dp/dt, and acceleration is the second derivative, a(t) = d2p/dt2. These are not abstract symbols; they correspond to sensors and actuators you use daily. For example, an IMU measures linear acceleration, encoders measure joint angular velocity, and GPS gives discretized position samples. When you compute derivatives numerically, be aware that differentiation amplifies noise — a common misconception is that derivative estimates always improve a controller. In practice, raw differentiation can make the signal worse; filtering or model-based estimation is often necessary. A concrete example: if x(t) = sin(t), then v(t) = cos(t) and a(t) = -sin(t). If your encoder reports small jitters, a derivative will magnify those spikes, leading to unstable control if used directly. Key takeaway: derivatives give the rates controllers need, but you must handle measurement noise and sampling carefully. Ask yourself: does my control loop expect instantaneous derivatives or filtered, estimated rates? Position, Velocity, Acceleration as Vector Derivatives means derivatives translate position into the rates controllers and sensors actually measure; treat numerical differentiation carefully because it amplifies noise.. In practical terms, mapping mathematical derivatives to sensors and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Rotation Rates and the Skew-Symmetric Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: When a rigid body rotates, its orientation can be expressed by a rotation matrix R(t). The rate at which R changes is not simply the derivative of angles but follows the matrix equation dR/dt = R times the skew-symmetric matrix Ω, which encodes angular velocity ω = [ωx, ωy, ωz]^T. The skew-symmetric form is Ω = [[0, -ωz, ωy],[ωz, 0, -ωx],[-ωy, ωx, 0]]. This relation is fundamental: it links the measured angular velocity from an IMU to the continuous update of orientation. A concrete example: for a rotation about the z-axis with ω = [0,0,ωz], Ω has only the -ωz and ωz off-diagonal entries, and the equation reduces to the familiar planar rotation derivative. A common misconception is to integrate individual Euler angles independently; that often leads to errors because rotation matrices do not commute and singularities can appear. Rather, integrate using the matrix relation or quaternions derived from ω. Key takeaway: dR/dt = RΩ gives a coordinate-free, robust method to propagate orientation from angular rate measurements, and it is the correct starting point for orientation integration in motion estimation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › Rotation Rates
Skew-symmetric Ω and dR/dt
dR/dt = R · Ω where Ω encodes angular velocity components and defines how orientation evolves.
Matrix form
Ω = [ 0   -ωz  ωy
      ωz   0   -ωx
     -ωy  ωx    0 ]
Analogy
Think of Ω as the generator of infinitesimal rotations; multiplying R by Ω gives the instantaneous change in orientation.
Common mistake
Integrating Euler angles separately ignores non-commutativity and can produce incorrect orientation over time.
Key Takeaway

Use RΩ propagation or quaternion integration to reliably update orientation from angular velocity measurements.

Concrete example
Rotation about z with ω=[0,0,ωz] yields Ω with entries ±ωz. Then dR/dt = RΩ simplifies to the planar rotation derivative used for yaw-only motion.
Try this
Integrate a small time step using R_next = R + dt * RΩ and re-orthogonalize R periodically to avoid numerical drift. Compare to quaternion-based integration.

screens.title: Velocity in a Rotating Frame and the Coriolis Term
screens.narratorSegment: When coordinates rotate, velocities measured in the rotating body frame do not directly equal velocities in the inertial world frame. The correct relation is v_world = v_body + omega cross r, where omega is the angular velocity of the body frame and r is the position of the point expressed in the body frame. This accounts for the extra apparent motion caused by the frame rotation. A concrete scenario: imagine a ball sliding on a rotating platform. If the ball is stationary relative to the platform, v_body is zero but v_world equals omega cross r, so an observer in the world frame sees the ball moving along a circle. This is the same physics underlying Coriolis effects experienced on rotating systems. A misconception is to treat velocities as invariant across frames; they are not. Another important point: when deriving equations of motion, these cross terms produce Coriolis and centripetal contributions that appear in the dynamics and affect controller design. Key takeaway: always include omega cross r when transforming velocities from body to world — omitting it yields incorrect predictions of inertial accelerations and can destabilize controllers.

v_world = v_body + ω × r
This relation captures how frame rotation adds apparent velocity to points fixed in the body.
Physical example
A point fixed at r on a rotating platform has zero body-frame velocity but nonzero world-frame velocity equal to ω × r.
Coriolis note

Key Takeaway

Transform velocities including the ω × r term to preserve physical correctness and avoid control errors.

screens.title: Ordinary Differential Equations in Robotics
screens.narratorSegment: An ordinary differential equation expresses how a system state changes over time. The canonical form is dx/dt = f(x, u, t), where x collects states such as positions, velocities, and orientations; u are control inputs like motor torques; and t is time. This formulation is how we encode robot dynamics for simulation and controller design. For instance, a simple pendulum's state x = [theta; omega] obeys dx/dt = [omega; -(g/L) sin(theta)], which couples angle and angular velocity in a nonlinear way. A common misconception is to expect closed-form analytical solutions for arbitrary robotic systems. In reality, many robotics ODEs are nonlinear and high dimensional, so we approximate solutions numerically. A concrete example: for a robotic joint with torque input τ, the second-order equation m d2q/dt2 + c dq/dt + k q = τ can be recast as a first-order system by defining velocity as an additional state. This conversion is essential because most numerical solvers operate on first-order systems. Takeaway: express dynamics as first-order ODEs to feed into numerical integrators and never assume linearity unless justified by the model. Ordinary Differential Equations in Robotics means always write dynamics in first-order ode form dx/dt = f(x,u,t) to prepare models for numerical integration and controller design.. In practical terms, state, input, and time: dx/dt = f(x, u, t). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Mass–Spring–Damper: From Second-Order to State-Space
screens.narratorSegment: A common mechanical model is the mass-spring-damper: m d2x/dt2 + c dx/dt + k x = F(t). To simulate this with standard ODE solvers, we convert it into a first-order system. Define state x1 = position and x2 = velocity, so the state vector becomes [x1; x2]. Then the first-order equations are dx1/dt = x2 and dx2/dt = (1/m) (F(t) - c x2 - k x1). This conversion clarifies how inputs and parameters affect each state. A concrete example: set m = 1, c = 0.5, k = 2 and F(t) = 0, with initial state x1(0)=1, x2(0)=0. The first-order system becomes dx/dt = [ x2; -0.5 x2 - 2 x1 ]. A common misconception is to treat the second-order form as incompatible with numerical solvers; in fact the conversion is mechanical and reversible, and most numerical libraries expect first-order form. Key takeaway: state augmentation is the standard bridge between physical second-order equations and solver-friendly first-order systems, and it preserves interpretation of position and velocity as separate states for controllers and observers. In practical terms, convert m d2x/dt2 + c dx/dt + k x = f(t) into a first-order system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Euler's Method — Simplicity and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Euler's method is the simplest numerical integrator: update the state by taking the derivative at the current point and stepping forward by dt. Its simplicity makes it easy to implement and fast per step, which is why beginners use it to learn integration. A concrete example: for dx/dt = -2x with x(0)=5, Euler with dt = 0.1 steps forward but will under- or overshoot depending on step size. The critical limitation is accuracy and stability. A common misconception is to assume that smaller dt always fixes all problems; while reducing dt improves accuracy, it also increases computation and can be insufficient for stiff systems where very small dt is required. For robotics, Euler with dt = 0.1 might show energy growth and diverging oscillations for a lightly damped oscillator; dt = 0.01 often behaves better but still lags compared to higher-order methods. The takeaway is to use Euler for quick prototyping, educational examples, and as a baseline, but prefer higher-order or adaptive solvers like RK4 or ode45 for reliable simulations in control development. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) — Better Accuracy Per Step
screens.narratorSegment: The 4th-order Runge-Kutta method, RK4, approximates the next state using four slope evaluations to form a weighted average. This gives much higher accuracy than Euler for the same time step. The typical RK4 step computes k1 = f(x), k2 = f(x + dt*k1/2), k3 = f(x + dt*k2/2), k4 = f(x + dt*k3), then x_next = x + dt*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)/6. A concrete benefit: for the same dt, RK4 often produces an order-of-magnitude smaller error than Euler, which is why it is a practical choice when fixed-step integrators are needed. A common misconception is that RK4 always eliminates the need to check dt; while RK4 is more accurate, extremely stiff systems can still force very small effective step sizes or require implicit methods. In MATLAB, implementing RK4 is straightforward as a step function; however, ode45 is an adaptive Runge-Kutta variant that usually outperforms fixed-step RK4 because it controls error automatically. Takeaway: use RK4 for fixed-step, improved accuracy, and use adaptive solvers when step size must vary to meet accuracy and stability constraints. content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.2 › RK4 Code
rk4_step function
Four intermediate evaluations form a stable, higher-order update for non-stiff problems.
function x_next = rk4_step(f, x, u, dt)
    k1 = f(x, u);
    k2 = f(x + dt*k1/2, u);
    k3 = f(x + dt*k2/2, u);
    k4 = f(x + dt*k3, u);
    x_next = x + dt*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)/6;
end
Notes
If input u changes with time, call f with appropriate time-shifted u for k2 and k3 evaluations. For stiff systems consider implicit alternatives.

% Define the dynamics of a simple pendulum

fullNarratorScript:
In robotics, calculus is the language that turns sensor readings into motion and control. In this chapter you will connect position, velocity, and acceleration as vector derivatives, learn how angular velocity drives orientation through a skew-symmetric matrix, and see how ordinary differential equations describe dynamics. You will also compare simple numerical integrators like Euler to higher-order methods like RK4, and run practical MATLAB simulations with ode45. These tools let you predict and test behavior before you run hardware, and they explain why some simulations explode while others remain stable. For example, a small time step in Euler's method may track a damped oscillator well, but a larger step can diverge and produce physically impossible energy growth. We will also examine rotating frames and the Coriolis term, which matter for quadrotors and any rotating mechanism. By the end, you will be able to set up the ODE for a mass-spring-damper, run an integration step, and reason about stability and solver choice. Consider the central idea: motion is derivatives, and derivatives integrated correctly give you reliable simulations.

These four objectives map directly to practical robotics tasks. First, you will compute derivatives and integrals of vector-valued functions to convert position signals into velocity and acceleration used by controllers and filters. Second, you will set up ordinary differential equations that model robot dynamics, expressing states and control inputs so you can reason about time evolution. Third, you will use numerical integrators such as Euler and Runge-Kutta to simulate dynamics in MATLAB and observe how step size affects accuracy. Fourth, you will understand velocity in rotating frames and the Coriolis contribution so you can correctly transform sensor data between body and inertial coordinates. Each objective explains a skill and why it matters: derivatives connect sensors to control; ODEs let you encode mechanics; numerical methods let you test algorithms offline; rotating-frame kinematics prevent errors in orientation-dependent forces. As you progress, you will see short examples and implement a damped oscillator simulation to verify understanding and experience stability trade-offs firsthand.

To verify your skills, each objective is paired with a small practical check. For derivatives, compute v(t) and a(t) for a given p(t) vector example and show units line up with sensor outputs. For ODE formulation, convert a second-order mass-spring-damper equation into a first-order state system and explain each state variable. For numerical integration, implement Euler and RK4 steps manually for one time step and compare them to the built-in solver result. For rotating frames, transform a measured body velocity to the world frame using v_world = v_body + omega cross r and explain the physical meaning of each term. These checks matter because they force you to connect equations to code and instruments. A successful verification shows not only correct math but also correct interpretation: you must explain the reason a large Euler time step fails, and why ode45 or a stiff solver might be chosen instead.

Start with a clear definition: position is a vector-valued function p(t) = [x(t), y(t), z(t)]^T that gives location in space over time. Velocity is its first derivative, v(t) = dp/dt, and acceleration is the second derivative, a(t) = d2p/dt2. These are not abstract symbols; they correspond to sensors and actuators you use daily. For example, an IMU measures linear acceleration, encoders measure joint angular velocity, and GPS gives discretized position samples. When you compute derivatives numerically, be aware that differentiation amplifies noise — a common misconception is that derivative estimates always improve a controller. In practice, raw differentiation can make the signal worse; filtering or model-based estimation is often necessary. A concrete example: if x(t) = sin(t), then v(t) = cos(t) and a(t) = -sin(t). If your encoder reports small jitters, a derivative will magnify those spikes, leading to unstable control if used directly. Key takeaway: derivatives give the rates controllers need, but you must handle measurement noise and sampling carefully. Ask yourself: does my control loop expect instantaneous derivatives or filtered, estimated rates? Position, Velocity, Acceleration as Vector Derivatives means derivatives translate position into the rates controllers and sensors actually measure; treat numerical differentiation carefully because it amplifies noise.. In practical terms, mapping mathematical derivatives to sensors and control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When a rigid body rotates, its orientation can be expressed by a rotation matrix R(t). The rate at which R changes is not simply the derivative of angles but follows the matrix equation dR/dt = R times the skew-symmetric matrix Ω, which encodes angular velocity ω = [ωx, ωy, ωz]^T. The skew-symmetric form is Ω = [[0, -ωz, ωy],[ωz, 0, -ωx],[-ωy, ωx, 0]]. This relation is fundamental: it links the measured angular velocity from an IMU to the continuous update of orientation. A concrete example: for a rotation about the z-axis with ω = [0,0,ωz], Ω has only the -ωz and ωz off-diagonal entries, and the equation reduces to the familiar planar rotation derivative. A common misconception is to integrate individual Euler angles independently; that often leads to errors because rotation matrices do not commute and singularities can appear. Rather, integrate using the matrix relation or quaternions derived from ω. Key takeaway: dR/dt = RΩ gives a coordinate-free, robust method to propagate orientation from angular rate measurements, and it is the correct starting point for orientation integration in motion estimation.

When coordinates rotate, velocities measured in the rotating body frame do not directly equal velocities in the inertial world frame. The correct relation is v_world = v_body + omega cross r, where omega is the angular velocity of the body frame and r is the position of the point expressed in the body frame. This accounts for the extra apparent motion caused by the frame rotation. A concrete scenario: imagine a ball sliding on a rotating platform. If the ball is stationary relative to the platform, v_body is zero but v_world equals omega cross r, so an observer in the world frame sees the ball moving along a circle. This is the same physics underlying Coriolis effects experienced on rotating systems. A misconception is to treat velocities as invariant across frames; they are not. Another important point: when deriving equations of motion, these cross terms produce Coriolis and centripetal contributions that appear in the dynamics and affect controller design. Key takeaway: always include omega cross r when transforming velocities from body to world — omitting it yields incorrect predictions of inertial accelerations and can destabilize controllers.

An ordinary differential equation expresses how a system state changes over time. The canonical form is dx/dt = f(x, u, t), where x collects states such as positions, velocities, and orientations; u are control inputs like motor torques; and t is time. This formulation is how we encode robot dynamics for simulation and controller design. For instance, a simple pendulum's state x = [theta; omega] obeys dx/dt = [omega; -(g/L) sin(theta)], which couples angle and angular velocity in a nonlinear way. A common misconception is to expect closed-form analytical solutions for arbitrary robotic systems. In reality, many robotics ODEs are nonlinear and high dimensional, so we approximate solutions numerically. A concrete example: for a robotic joint with torque input τ, the second-order equation m d2q/dt2 + c dq/dt + k q = τ can be recast as a first-order system by defining velocity as an additional state. This conversion is essential because most numerical solvers operate on first-order systems. Euler's method is the simplest numerical integrator: update the state by taking the derivative at the current point and stepping forward by dt. Its simplicity makes it easy to implement and fast per step, which is why beginners use it to learn integration. A concrete example: for dx/dt = -2x with x(0)=5, Euler with dt = 0.1 steps forward but will under- or overshoot depending on step size. The critical limitation is accuracy and stability. A common misconception is to assume that smaller dt always fixes all problems; while reducing dt improves accuracy, it also increases computation and can be insufficient for stiff systems where very small dt is required. For robotics, Euler with dt = 0.1 might show energy growth and diverging oscillations for a lightly damped oscillator; dt = 0.01 often behaves better but still lags compared to higher-order methods. The takeaway is to use Euler for quick prototyping, educational examples, and as a baseline, but prefer higher-order or adaptive solvers like RK4 or ode45 for reliable simulations in control development. The 4th-order Runge-Kutta method, RK4, approximates the next state using four slope evaluations to form a weighted average. This gives much higher accuracy than Euler for the same time step. The typical RK4 step computes k1 = f(x), k2 = f(x + dt*k1/2), k3 = f(x + dt*k2/2), k4 = f(x + dt*k3), then x_next = x + dt*(k1 + 2*k2 + 2*k3 + k4)/6. A concrete benefit: for the same dt, RK4 often produces an order-of-magnitude smaller error than Euler, which is why it is a practical choice when fixed-step integrators are needed. A common misconception is that RK4 always eliminates the need to check dt; while RK4 is more accurate, extremely stiff systems can still force very small effective step sizes or require implicit methods. In MATLAB, implementing RK4 is straightforward as a step function; however, ode45 is an adaptive Runge-Kutta variant that usually outperforms fixed-step RK4 because it controls error automatically. Takeaway: use RK4 for fixed-step, improved accuracy, and use adaptive solvers when step size must vary to meet accuracy and stability constraints.
